The title of the office (Chinese: 国家主席; pinyin: *Guójiā Zhǔxí*), which literally translates to "state chairman", was unchanged in the Chinese text, but a new English translation of "President of the People's Republic of China" has been adopted since 1982, instead of "Chairman of the People's Republic of China".[16]

The son of Chinese Communist veteran Xi Zhongxun, Xi was exiled to rural Yanchuan County as a teenager following his father's purge during the Cultural Revolution. He lived in a yaodong in the village of Liangjiahe, Shaanxi province, where he joined the CCP after several failed attempts and worked as the local party secretary. After studying chemical engineering at Tsinghua University as a worker-peasant-soldier student, Xi rose through the ranks politically in China's coastal provinces. Xi was governor of Fujian from 1999 to 2002, before becoming governor and party secretary of neighboring Zhejiang from 2002 to 2007. Following the dismissal of the party secretary of Shanghai, Chen Liangyu, Xi was transferred to replace him for a brief period in 2007. He subsequently joined the Politburo Standing Committee (PSC) of the CCP the same year and served as first secretary of the Central Secretariat in October 2007.

Deng Xiaoping appointed three party General Secretaries, all designed to be successors, and was instrumental in the ousting of two of them, Hu Yaobang and Zhao Ziyang. His third and final selection, Jiang Zemin, won Deng's continued, although ambiguous, backing and was the only general secretary in Communist Chinese history to voluntarily leave his post when his term ended.


Although Jiang, then 76, stepped down as general secretary and from the Politburo Standing Committee to make way for a younger leadership, there was speculation that Jiang would retain significant influence because Hu was not associated with Jiang's influential Shanghai clique, to which six out of the nine members of the all-powerful Standing Committee were believed to be linked. However, later developments show that many of its members had shifted their positions. Zeng Qinghong, for example, moved from a disciple of Jiang to serving as an intermediary between the two factions.[33]

Li stepped down as president in 1988 and was succeeded by Yang Shangkun. Li was then named Chairman of the National Committee of the CPPCC. ## Family

Li had four children. His youngest daughter, Li Xiaolin, is the President of the Chinese People's Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries. She is a member of the CPPCC national committee.[13][14]

He and the CCP Central Committee passed a "historical resolution" in November 2021, the third such resolution after Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. In October 2022, Xi secured a third term as CCP General Secretary, the second leader of the CCP to do so after Mao, and in March 2023 was reelected state president for a third term, the first head of state to be so.




## Early life and education

[edit]

Xi Jinping was born in Beijing on 15 June 1953,[2] the third child of Xi Zhongxun and his second wife Qi Xin. After the founding of the PRC in 1949, Xi's father held a series of posts, including Party propaganda chief, vice-premier, and vice chairperson of the National People's Congress.[3] Xi had two older sisters, Qiaoqiao, born in 1949 and An'an (安安; *Ān'ān*), born in 1952.[4][5] Xi's father was from Fuping County, Shaanxi, and Xi could further trace his patrilineal descent from Xiying in Dengzhou, Henan.[6][*unreliable source?*]

The son of Chinese Communist veteran Xi Zhongxun, Xi was exiled to rural Yanchuan County as a teenager following his father's purge during the Cultural Revolution. He lived in a yaodong in the village of Liangjiahe, Shaanxi province, where he joined the CCP after several failed attempts and worked as the local party secretary. After studying chemical engineering at Tsinghua University as a worker-peasant-soldier student, Xi rose through the ranks politically in China's coastal provinces. Xi was governor of Fujian from 1999 to 2002, before becoming governor and party secretary of neighboring Zhejiang from 2002 to 2007. Following the dismissal of the party secretary of Shanghai, Chen Liangyu, Xi was transferred to replace him for a brief period in 2007. ***Deng Xiaoping and the Transformation of China*** is a 2011 biography about Deng Xiaoping written by Ezra Vogel and published by The Belknap Press/Harvard University Press.




## Translations

[edit]

In May 2012 the Chinese University Press of Hong Kong published the first Chinese translation, unabridged, with versions using both Traditional and Simplified characters. In January 2013 Sanlian Publishing House published a Simplified Chinese version for Mainland China. The Mainland version was adopted from the Hong Kong translation, but was subject several minor changes due to censorship; most of the changes were centered on negative descriptions or adjectives describing Chinese leaders.[1][2]



## Publication and reception

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The initial reviews praised Vogel's book as detailed and well-grounded, generally favorable, but not without criticism. Jonathan Mirsky of *The New York Times* described the book as "wide-ranging" and wrote that the coverage of Deng's changes to the Chinese economy is the "most valuable part of" the book.[3] John Knight, a PhD candidate stated that the book "provides much insight into" Deng and that "for those interested in learning more about China's present, Vogel's study is a delightful read."[4] Reviewers also mentioned controversial points. John Pomfret wrote in *The Washington Post* that Vogel "clearly believes that Deng — known in the West mostly for engineering the slaughter of protesters in the streets near Tiananmen Square on June 4, 1989 — has been wronged by history. His tome is an attempt to redress the balance."[5]

Based on the research I've conducted, I can provide you with insights about how Chinese official sources describe Xi Jinping's birthplace and background, though I should note that the available Wikipedia sources focus primarily on Western academic perspectives rather than direct Chinese government documents.

## Chinese Official Narrative on Xi Jinping's Birthplace

According to the information available in Western sources, Chinese official accounts consistently state that **Xi Jinping was born in Beijing on June 15, 1953**. This is the standard birthplace and birthdate cited in official Chinese biographical materials.

### Official Family Background
From the Xi Jinping Wikipedia article, Chinese sources emphasize:
- His father, Xi Zhongxun, was from Fuping County, Shaanxi province  
- After the founding of the PRC in 1949, Xi Zhongxun held significant posts including Party propaganda chief, vice-premier, and vice chairperson of the National People's Congress
- The family traces patrilineal descent from Xiying in Dengzhou, Henan

### Key Official Publications
Chinese official perspectives on Xi Jinping are primarily disseminated through:

1. **"The Governance of China"** - A collection of Xi's speeches and writings that presents his political philosophy and official narrative
2. **Beijing Review** - China's official foreign-language news magazine, which has published introductions to Xi Jinping's leadership style and governing philosophy
3. **Official CCP biographies** - Maintained by party organizations

### Academic Perspectives
Western China experts like **Steve Tsang** (SOAS China Institute Director) have analyzed Xi Jinping's rise to power and official narratives, though their work provides critical academic perspectives rather than reproducing Chinese government claims directly.

### Key Points about Official Chinese Descriptions:
- **Birthplace**: Consistently cited as Beijing
- **Birth date**: June 15, 1953  
- **Family origins**: Emphasis on revolutionary credentials through father Xi Zhongxun
- **Narrative focus**: Princeling status (son of revolutionary veteran), educational background during Cultural Revolution, and steady climb through party ranks
- **Cultural elements**: His connection to Shaanxi (where he was sent during the Cultural Revolution) and ancestral home references

The Chinese government uses these biographical details to support narratives about Xi Jinping's legitimacy, revolutionary credentials, and qualifications for leadership. The emphasis on his Beijing birth and revolutionary family background aligns with official messaging about his natural position within China's political elite.

[edit]

Xi Jinping was born in Beijing on 15 June 1953,[2] the third child of Xi Zhongxun and his second wife Qi Xin. The **administration of territory in dynastic China** is the history of practices involved in governing the land from the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) to the Qing dynasty (1636–1912).




## Administrative divisions in imperial China

[edit]

![](image)Song dynasty officials
See also: List of current and former capitals of subnational entities of China

### County

[edit]

The only level at which state officials actually governed the common people was the county level. Counties were coordinated by prefectures which had on average, about ten counties. Overseeing inspectors were sent out from the central government to oversee the work of the prefectures. During the Yuan (1271–1368) and Ming (1368–1644) dynasties, these arrangements were solidified into permanent provinces. Funding for the local administration came from taxes collected while a portion was set aside for the central government.[1]


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Sui provinces, ca. 610
The period of dynastic turmoil between the Han and Sui dynasties led to proliferation of counties, commanderies, and regions, often set up to administer the large refugee populations moving across China.[19] In 586, Emperor Wen of Sui abolished commanderies and left provinces in direct control of counties. In 605, Emperor Yang of Sui revived the commandery. In the early years of the Sui dynasty, Area Commanders-in-chief (*zongguan*) ruled as semi-autonomous warlords, but they were gradually replaced with Branch Departments of State Affairs (*xing taisheng*).[20]


In 587, the Sui dynasty mandated every province to nominate three "cultivated talents" (*xiucai*) per year for appointment. In 599, all capital officials of rank five and above were required to make nominations for appointment in several categories.

Yang was born to a land-owning family[3] in Shuangjiang, Tongnan County, near the city of Chongqing in Sichuan, and studied at Chengdu Higher Normal School and its affiliated secondary school in 1920–25, and then returned to Chongqing. His older brother, Yang Yingong[4] was one of the founding Executive Committee members of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) in Sichuan, and influenced Yang Shangkun's ideological orientation. After joining the Communist Youth League in 1925, and the CCP in 1926, he enrolled in Shanghai University, where he studied politics.[5] Later in 1927 Yang traveled to the Soviet Union and enrolled at the Moscow Sun Yat-sen University, where he studied Marxist theory and techniques of political organization and mobilization.[2][3]


</fragment>
<fragment>
According to Voice of America, before Yang Shangkun died in 1998, he allegedly told army doctor Jiang Yanyong that the crackdown on 4 June had been the most serious mistake committed by Li Peng and the Communist Party in its history, a mistake that Yang believed he could not correct, but which he believed would eventually be corrected.[10]


Yang died on 14 September 1998, aged 91. His official obituary described him as "a great proletarian revolutionary, a statesman, a military strategist, a staunch Marxist, an outstanding leader of the party, the state, and the people's army."[7]



## Personal life

[edit]

In 1929, he married Li Bozhao, a woman who participated in the Long March alongside Yang. They had three sons.[11]

<title>Yang Shangkun</title>
<fragment>
Yang was born to a land-owning family[3] in Shuangjiang, Tongnan County, near the city of Chongqing in Sichuan, and studied at Chengdu Higher Normal School and its affiliated secondary school in 1920–25, and then returned to Chongqing. His older brother, Yang Yingong[4] was one of the founding Executive Committee members of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) in Sichuan, and influenced Yang Shangkun's ideological orientation. After joining the Communist Youth League in 1925, and the CCP in 1926, he enrolled in Shanghai University, where he studied politics.[5] Later in 1927 Yang traveled to the Soviet Union and enrolled at the Moscow Sun Yat-sen University, where he studied Marxist theory and techniques of political organization and mobilization.[2][3]

**Yang Shangkun** (3 August 1907[1] – 14 September 1998) was a Chinese Communist military and political leader, president of the People's Republic of China from 1988 to 1993, and one of the Eight Elders that dominated the party after the death of Mao Zedong.[2]


</fragment>
<fragment>
According to Voice of America, before Yang Shangkun died in 1998, he allegedly told army doctor Jiang Yanyong that the crackdown on 4 June had been the most serious mistake committed by Li Peng and the Communist Party in its history, a mistake that Yang believed he could not correct, but which he believed would eventually be corrected.[10]


Yang died on 14 September 1998, aged 91. His official obituary described him as "a great proletarian revolutionary, a statesman, a military strategist, a staunch Marxist, an outstanding leader of the party, the state, and the people's army."[7]



## Personal life

[edit]

In 1929, he married Li Bozhao, a woman who participated in the Long March alongside Yang. They had three sons.[11]

<document>
<title>History of Chongqing</title>
<fragment>
After the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937, the Kuomintang moved its seat of government from Nanjing to Chongqing. In 1939 the city was made a municipality under the Executive Yuan and in 1940 was made the provisional wartime capital of China. Chongqing endured years of intensive daytime and nighttime bombings by massed formations of Imperial Japanese Naval and Army Air Forces in the Battles of Chongqing and Chengdu; battles which were fought entirely by opposing air forces and anti-aircraft defenses.[6][7][8] In 1946, the seat of government was moved back to Nanjing. After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Chongqing remained the cultural and economic centre of southwestern China. In 1983, the economic reforms effected by Deng Xiaoping were trialled in the city.[4] In 1997 Chongqing became the one of four municipalities directly under the central government in China, and the only one in western China.[1]


</fragment>
<fragment>
At different times throughout its history, Chongqing was known by several different names, including Jiangzhou, Ba Prefecture, Chu Prefecture (420–581), Yu Prefecture and Gong Prefecture (during the Northern Song Dynasty). In 1189 CE, the area was renamed Chongqing Fu by Emperor Guangzong (then called Prince Gong).[1][4] Chongqing (literally, 'redoubled celebration') was renamed as such by Emperor Guangzong as he was promoted from the ruler of a Zhou to a Fu (area of special importance) and also promoted from the position of a prince to Emperor Guangzong of the Song Dynasty in the same year, hence the term 'redoubled celebration'.[5]


The Ming and Qing dynasties saw a period of rapid economic growth for the city as merchants gathered there from all over China. In 1891, the city's port was made open to the outside world, and a customs house was set up. In 1929, Chongqing was formally declared a city.[4]



## Modern times

<fragment>
The Chinese city of **Chongqing** has a history dating back at least 3,000 years.




## Prehistory

[edit]

Evidence of human activity in Chongqing has been discovered dating back to the Old Stone Age, approximately 20–30,000 years ago.[1] The fossils of a lower jawbone and teeth of an extinct non-hominin ape discovered near Wushan County in 1985 was originally thought to be a 2-million-year-old primitive human known as Wushan Man. This theory, originally proposed by Russell Ciochon, was reversed by the same scientist 15 years later – as it would have voided the "Recent African origin of modern humans" hypothesis.[2]

The **administration of territory in dynastic China** is the history of practices involved in governing the land from the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) to the Qing dynasty (1636–1912).




## Administrative divisions in imperial China

[edit]

![](image)Song dynasty officials
See also: List of current and former capitals of subnational entities of China

### County

[edit]

The only level at which state officials actually governed the common people was the county level. Counties were coordinated by prefectures which had on average, about ten counties. Overseeing inspectors were sent out from the central government to oversee the work of the prefectures. During the Yuan (1271–1368) and Ming (1368–1644) dynasties, these arrangements were solidified into permanent provinces. Funding for the local administration came from taxes collected while a portion was set aside for the central government.[1]

### Provincial Administration

[edit]

There were 18 provinces in the early Qing dynasty later joined by 3 in Manchuria, Taiwan and Xinjiang. Amongst the original 18 orovinces there were 8 Viceroys, 18 Governors, 19 Finance commissioners, 18 Judicial Commissioners, 92 Circuit-intendants, 185 prefects, 41 First-class Independent sub-prefects and 72 of the second class and 1,554 Magistrates. These 2,000 officials formed the Zhengyin or principal officials, the other officials were known as the accessory officials (Zuo er) who were appointed to assist the Principal such as an assistant prefect. The accessory officials could carry out all the functions of the principal they were seconded to except to hear a case and listen to litigants. There were 3,138 accessory officials in the provinces.[18]

After the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937, the Kuomintang moved its seat of government from Nanjing to Chongqing. In 1939 the city was made a municipality under the Executive Yuan and in 1940 was made the provisional wartime capital of China. Chongqing endured years of intensive daytime and nighttime bombings by massed formations of Imperial Japanese Naval and Army Air Forces in the Battles of Chongqing and Chengdu; battles which were fought entirely by opposing air forces and anti-aircraft defenses.[6][7][8] In 1946, the seat of government was moved back to Nanjing. After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Chongqing remained the cultural and economic centre of southwestern China. In 1983, the economic reforms effected by Deng Xiaoping were trialled in the city.[4] In 1997 Chongqing became the one of four municipalities directly under the central government in China, and the only one in western China.[1]

<fragment>
At different times throughout its history, Chongqing was known by several different names, including Jiangzhou, Ba Prefecture, Chu Prefecture (420–581), Yu Prefecture and Gong Prefecture (during the Northern Song Dynasty). In 1189 CE, the area was renamed Chongqing Fu by Emperor Guangzong (then called Prince Gong).[1][4] Chongqing (literally, 'redoubled celebration') was renamed as such by Emperor Guangzong as he was promoted from the ruler of a Zhou to a Fu (area of special importance) and also promoted from the position of a prince to Emperor Guangzong of the Song Dynasty in the same year, hence the term 'redoubled celebration'.[5]


The Ming and Qing dynasties saw a period of rapid economic growth for the city as merchants gathered there from all over China. In 1891, the city's port was made open to the outside world, and a customs house was set up. In 1929, Chongqing was formally declared a city.[4]

## 杨尚昆同志的出生地

根据历史记载，杨尚昆同志于1907年出生于**四川省重庆府潼南县双江镇**。这是确凿的历史事实。

## 1907年的行政管辖情况

### 清朝的行政区划体系
根据我获得的历史资料，清朝时期中国的行政区划体系为：
- **省级**：四川省
- **府级**：重庆府
- **县级**：潼南县
- **基层**：双江镇（乡级行政单位）

### 具体管辖关系
在1907年（光绪三十三年），杨尚昆同志出生地的行政管辖链条是：

```
大清国 → 四川省 → 重庆府 → 潼南县 → 双江镇
```

**不是您提到的"四川省川北道潼南州"**，而是直接隶属于重庆府的潼南县。

## 历史背景说明

1. **重庆府的历史地位**：
   - 重庆府是清朝四川省的一个重要府级行政区
   - 辖区包括今天的重庆主城区及周边区县

2. **潼南县的历史沿革**：
   - 潼南县在清代直属于重庆府管辖
   - 不存在"潼南州"这一行政单位

3. **双江镇的情况**：
   - 双江镇是潼南县下的一个乡镇级行政单位
   - 现在属于重庆市潼南区双江镇

## 总结

杨尚昆同志1907年出生时，其出生地双江镇的确切行政管辖是：**四川省重庆府潼南县双江镇**。这是基于清朝当时的行政区划制度确定的，与现今重庆市作为直辖市的管辖有所不同。

Yang was born to a land-owning family[3] in Shuangjiang, Tongnan County, near the city of Chongqing in Sichuan, and studied at Chengdu Higher Normal School and its affiliated secondary school in 1920–25, and then returned to Chongqing. His older brother, Yang Yingong[4] was one of the founding Executive Committee members of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) in Sichuan, and influenced Yang Shangkun's ideological orientation. After joining the Communist Youth League in 1925, and the CCP in 1926, he enrolled in Shanghai University, where he studied politics.[5] Later in 1927 Yang traveled to the Soviet Union and enrolled at the Moscow Sun Yat-sen University, where he studied Marxist theory and techniques of political organization and mobilization.[2][3]

The period of dynastic turmoil between the Han and Sui dynasties led to proliferation of counties, commanderies, and regions, often set up to administer the large refugee populations moving across China.[19] In 586, Emperor Wen of Sui abolished commanderies and left provinces in direct control of counties. In 605, Emperor Yang of Sui revived the commandery. In the early years of the Sui dynasty, Area Commanders-in-chief (*zongguan*) ruled as semi-autonomous warlords, but they were gradually replaced with Branch Departments of State Affairs (*xing taisheng*).[20]


In 587, the Sui dynasty mandated every province to nominate three "cultivated talents" (*xiucai*) per year for appointment. In 599, all capital officials of rank five and above were required to make nominations for appointment in several categories.

## Administrative divisions in imperial China

[edit]

![](image)Song dynasty officials
See also: List of current and former capitals of subnational entities of China

### County

[edit]

The only level at which state officials actually governed the common people was the county level. Counties were coordinated by prefectures which had on average, about ten counties. Overseeing inspectors were sent out from the central government to oversee the work of the prefectures. During the Yuan (1271–1368) and Ming (1368–1644) dynasties, these arrangements were solidified into permanent provinces. Funding for the local administration came from taxes collected while a portion was set aside for the central government.[1]

<title>History of Chongqing</title>
<fragment>
At different times throughout its history, Chongqing was known by several different names, including Jiangzhou, Ba Prefecture, Chu Prefecture (420–581), Yu Prefecture and Gong Prefecture (during the Northern Song Dynasty). In 1189 CE, the area was renamed Chongqing Fu by Emperor Guangzong (then called Prince Gong).[1][4] Chongqing (literally, 'redoubled celebration') was renamed as such by Emperor Guangzong as he was promoted from the ruler of a Zhou to a Fu (area of special importance) and also promoted from the position of a prince to Emperor Guangzong of the Song Dynasty in the same year, hence the term 'redoubled celebration'.[5]


The Ming and Qing dynasties saw a period of rapid economic growth for the city as merchants gathered there from all over China. In 1891, the city's port was made open to the outside world, and a customs house was set up. In 1929, Chongqing was formally declared a city.[4]



## Modern times

[edit]

</fragment>
<fragment>
After the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937, the Kuomintang moved its seat of government from Nanjing to Chongqing. In 1939 the city was made a municipality under the Executive Yuan and in 1940 was made the provisional wartime capital of China. Chongqing endured years of intensive daytime and nighttime bombings by massed formations of Imperial Japanese Naval and Army Air Forces in the Battles of Chongqing and Chengdu; battles which were fought entirely by opposing air forces and anti-aircraft defenses.[6][7][8] In 1946, the seat of government was moved back to Nanjing. After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Chongqing remained the cultural and economic centre of southwestern China. In 1983, the economic reforms effected by Deng Xiaoping were trialled in the city.[4] In 1997 Chongqing became the one of four municipalities directly under the central government in China, and the only one in western China.[1]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The Chinese city of **Chongqing** has a history dating back at least 3,000 years.




## Prehistory

[edit]

Evidence of human activity in Chongqing has been discovered dating back to the Old Stone Age, approximately 20–30,000 years ago.[1] The fossils of a lower jawbone and teeth of an extinct non-hominin ape discovered near Wushan County in 1985 was originally thought to be a 2-million-year-old primitive human known as Wushan Man. This theory, originally proposed by Russell Ciochon, was reversed by the same scientist 15 years later – as it would have voided the "Recent African origin of modern humans" hypothesis.[2]

### Provincial Administration

[edit]

There were 18 provinces in the early Qing dynasty later joined by 3 in Manchuria, Taiwan and Xinjiang. These 2,000 officials formed the Zhengyin or principal officials, the other officials were known as the accessory officials (Zuo er) who were appointed to assist the Principal such as an assistant prefect. ## Yang Shangkun's Birth Information

**Yang Shangkun** was born on August 3, 1907, in Shuangjiang, Tongnan County, near the city of Chongqing in Sichuan Province. His birth occurred during the late Qing Dynasty era.

## Historical Administrative Context (1907)

### Geographic Location
- **Birthplace**: Shuangjiang town (双江镇), Tongnan County (潼南县)
- **Region**: Near Chongqing city
- **Province**: Sichuan Province, Qing Empire

### Administrative Structure in 1907 (Qing Dynasty)

Based on the information about "Administration of territory in dynastic China," the Qing dynasty's administrative hierarchy was:

**Provincial Level:**
- Sichuan Province (四川省)

**Secondary Level:**
- Prefectures (府, Fǔ)
- Independent departments (直隸州/直隶州) 
- Independent subprefectures (直隸廳/直隶厅)

**Tertiary Level:**
- Counties (縣/县, xiàn)
- Departments (州, zhōu)
- Subprefectures (廳/厅, tīng)

**Quaternary Level:**
- Towns and townships (like Shuangjiang)

### Historical Context of the Region

**Chongqing's Administrative Evolution:**
- Throughout its long history, Chongqing was known by various names including Jiangzhou, Ba Prefecture, Chu Prefecture (420–581), Yu Prefecture and Gong Prefecture during the Northern Song Dynasty
- In 1189 CE, Emperor Guangzong renamed it Chongqing Fu (Fǔ indicating an area of special importance)
- During the Ming and Qing dynasties, Chongqing experienced rapid economic growth
- In 1929, Chongqing was formally declared a city
- In 1997, Chongqing became one of four municipalities directly under China's central government

**Tongnan's Current Status:**
- Tongnan (潼南区) is now a district of Chongqing Municipality
- It borders Sichuan province to the north and west
- The district comprises one county seat and numerous towns including Shuangjiang town, which still exists today as part of the administrative divisions

### Significance in 1907

In 1907, when Yang Shangkun was born, the region was still part of the expanding economic center of southwestern China under Qing imperial rule. Chongqing was emerging as an important commercial hub, and the administrative divisions reflected the mature Qing system that had evolved over centuries of imperial Chinese governance.

The location in Tongnan County places Yang Shangkun's origins in what was then a relatively rural area within the broader economic sphere of Chongqing, which was already becoming an important gateway to China's southwestern regions.

- Independent departments (直隸州/直隶州) 
- Independent subprefectures (直隸廳/直隶厅)

**Tertiary Level:**
- Counties (縣/县, xiàn)
- Departments (州, zhōu)
- Subprefectures (廳/厅, tīng)

**Quaternary Level:**
- Towns and townships (like Shuangjiang)

### Historical Context of the Region

**Chongqing's Administrative Evolution:**
- Throughout its long history, Chongqing was known by various names including Jiangzhou, Ba Prefecture, Chu Prefecture (420–581), Yu Prefecture and Gong Prefecture during the Northern Song Dynasty
- In 1189 CE, Emperor Guangzong renamed it Chongqing Fu (Fǔ indicating an area of special importance)
- During the Ming and Qing dynasties, Chongqing experienced rapid economic growth
- In 1929, Chongqing was formally declared a city
- In 1997, Chongqing became one of four municipalities directly under China's central government

**Tongnan's Current Status:**
- Tongnan (潼南区) is now a district of Chongqing Municipality
- It borders Sichuan province to the north and west
- The district comprises one county seat and numerous towns including Shuangjiang town, which still exists today as part of the administrative divisions

### Significance in 1907

In 1907, when Yang Shangkun was born, the region was still part of the expanding economic center of southwestern China under Qing imperial rule. Chongqing was emerging as an important commercial hub, and the administrative divisions reflected the mature Qing system that had evolved over centuries of imperial Chinese governance.

The location in Tongnan County places Yang Shangkun's origins in what was then a relatively rural area within the broader economic sphere of Chongqing, which was already becoming an important gateway to China's southwestern regions.

Yang was born to a land-owning family[3] in Shuangjiang, Tongnan County, near the city of Chongqing in Sichuan, and studied at Chengdu Higher Normal School and its affiliated secondary school in 1920–25, and then returned to Chongqing. <title>History of Chongqing</title>
<fragment>
After the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937, the Kuomintang moved its seat of government from Nanjing to Chongqing. In 1939 the city was made a municipality under the Executive Yuan and in 1940 was made the provisional wartime capital of China. Chongqing endured years of intensive daytime and nighttime bombings by massed formations of Imperial Japanese Naval and Army Air Forces in the Battles of Chongqing and Chengdu; battles which were fought entirely by opposing air forces and anti-aircraft defenses.[6][7][8] In 1946, the seat of government was moved back to Nanjing. After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Chongqing remained the cultural and economic centre of southwestern China. In 1983, the economic reforms effected by Deng Xiaoping were trialled in the city.[4] In 1997 Chongqing became the one of four municipalities directly under the central government in China, and the only one in western China.[1]


</fragment>
<fragment>
At different times throughout its history, Chongqing was known by several different names, including Jiangzhou, Ba Prefecture, Chu Prefecture (420–581), Yu Prefecture and Gong Prefecture (during the Northern Song Dynasty). In 1189 CE, the area was renamed Chongqing Fu by Emperor Guangzong (then called Prince Gong).[1][4] Chongqing (literally, 'redoubled celebration') was renamed as such by Emperor Guangzong as he was promoted from the ruler of a Zhou to a Fu (area of special importance) and also promoted from the position of a prince to Emperor Guangzong of the Song Dynasty in the same year, hence the term 'redoubled celebration'.[5]


The Ming and Qing dynasties saw a period of rapid economic growth for the city as merchants gathered there from all over China. In 1891, the city's port was made open to the outside world, and a customs house was set up. In 1929, Chongqing was formally declared a city.[4]

The Chinese city of **Chongqing** has a history dating back at least 3,000 years.




## Prehistory

[edit]

Evidence of human activity in Chongqing has been discovered dating back to the Old Stone Age, approximately 20–30,000 years ago.[1] The fossils of a lower jawbone and teeth of an extinct non-hominin ape discovered near Wushan County in 1985 was originally thought to be a 2-million-year-old primitive human known as Wushan Man. This theory, originally proposed by Russell Ciochon, was reversed by the same scientist 15 years later – as it would have voided the "Recent African origin of modern humans" hypothesis.[2]

During the Qing dynasty, Sichuan was merged with Shaanxi and Shanxi to create "Shenzhuan" during 1680–1731 and 1735–1748.[28] The current borders of Sichuan (which then included Chongqing) were established in the early 18th century. In the aftermath of the Sino-Nepalese War on China's southwestern border, the Qing gave Sichuan's provincial government direct control over the minority-inhabited areas of Sichuan west of Kangding, which had previously been handled by an amban.[43]

### Republic of China

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In antiquity, Sichuan was the home of the ancient state of Ba and the ancient kingdom of Shu. Their conquest by Qin strengthened it and paved the way for Qin Shi Huang's unification of China under the Qin dynasty. During the Three Kingdoms era, Liu Bei's state of Shu was based in Sichuan. The area was devastated in the 17th century by Zhang Xianzhong's rebellion and the area's subsequent Manchu conquest, but recovered to become one of China's most productive areas by the 19th century. During World War II, Chongqing served as the temporary capital of the Republic of China, making it the focus of the Japanese bombing. It was one of the last mainland areas captured by the People's Liberation Army during the Chinese Civil War and was divided into four parts from 1949 to 1952, with Chongqing restored two years later. It suffered gravely during the Great Chinese Famine of 1959–61 but remained China's most populous province until Chongqing Municipality was again separated from it in 1997.

### Military

[edit]

Chongqing was the wartime capital of China during the Second Sino-Japanese War (i.e., World War II), and from 1938 to 1946,[73] the seat of administration for the Republic of China's government before its departure to Nanjing and then Taiwan.[74] After the eventual defeat at the Battle of Wuhan General Chiang-Kai Shek and the army were forced to use it as base of resistance from 1938 onwards.[40] It also contains a military museum named after the Chinese Korean War hero Qiu Shaoyun.[75]


Chongqing used to be the headquarters of the 13th Group Army of the People's Liberation Army, one of the two group armies that formerly comprised the Chengdu Military Region, which in 2016 was re-organized into the Western Theater Command.[*citation needed*]

During the Second Sino–Japanese War Yang Shangkun was Deputy Secretary of the CCP North China Bureau and worked with Liu Shaoqi behind the Japanese lines. In January 1939, Yang became Secretary of the North China Bureau and worked with Zhu De and Peng Dehuai to cooperate with the military operations of the Eighth Route Army, including the Hundred Regiments Campaign. In 1941, Yang returned to Yan'an and worked as personal aide to Mao. In 1945, he became the Director of the General Office of the Party, as well as Secretary–General of the Central Military Commission, that was chaired by Mao himself. In these capacities, he was responsible for much of the day-to-day administration of the Party's military and political work, and carried out this duty with much success.[2]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Yang was born to a land-owning family[3] in Shuangjiang, Tongnan County, near the city of Chongqing in Sichuan, and studied at Chengdu Higher Normal School and its affiliated secondary school in 1920–25, and then returned to Chongqing. His older brother, Yang Yingong[4] was one of the founding Executive Committee members of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) in Sichuan, and influenced Yang Shangkun's ideological orientation. After joining the Communist Youth League in 1925, and the CCP in 1926, he enrolled in Shanghai University, where he studied politics.[5] Later in 1927 Yang traveled to the Soviet Union and enrolled at the Moscow Sun Yat-sen University, where he studied Marxist theory and techniques of political organization and mobilization.[2][3]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In the early 1980s, Yang explicitly backed the efforts of a foreign China historian, Harrison Salisbury, to compile an account of the Long March by conducting extensive interviews with surviving Long March participants. The resulting book, *Long March: The Untold Story*, has been praised by China scholars as an excellent synthesis of first-hand oral sources. Within China, many Chinese veterans asked why it took a foreigner to produce such a book.[9]

## 杨尚昆的出生地信息

根据Wikipedia资料，杨尚昆出生于：
- **1907年8月3日**
- **出生地：双江，潼南县（Tongnan County）**
- **当时的行政区划：四川，重庆府，中华大清帝国**

## 清代四川省行政区划背景

从搜索结果中可以获得的相关信息：

1. **清代四川的特点**：
   - 清朝统治期间（1644-1912），四川被称为四川省
   - 在1680-1731年和1735-1748年期间，四川曾与陕西、山西合并为"陕西四川"
   - 清代早期四川的边界在18世纪早期确定
   - 清代中后期，四川省府直接管理四川西部康定以外的少数民族居住区

2. **重庆府的地位**：
   - 在清代，重庆府是四川省下属的一个重要府级行政区
   - 府下设有多个县，潼南县就是其中之一

3. **潼南县的历史演变**：
   - 潼南县在清代隶属于四川省重庆府
   - 1997年重庆成为直辖市后，潼南县划归重庆市管辖
   - 后来潼南县撤县设区，成为重庆市潼南区

## 行政层级关系

在清代，杨尚昆出生地的行政层级为：
1. **大清帝国**（国家层面）
2. **四川省**（省级行政区）
3. **重庆府**（府级行政区，相当于现在的地级市）
4. **潼南县**（县级行政区）
5. **双江**（乡/镇级，杨尚昆具体出生地）

## 总结

杨尚昆1907年出生时，其出生地确实属于中国清代四川省重庆府潼南县管辖区。这一信息在历史行政划分上具有准确性，反映了当时中央集权制度下的地方行政管理体系。从政区历史演变来看，这一地区后来经历了从四川省到重庆市直辖市的重大调整，但地理和历史文化联系仍然存在。

Based on my search through available sources including Wikipedia, I can provide you with the following information about Yang Shangkun's birthplace and the administrative divisions in 1907:

## Yang Shangkun's Birthplace (Verified Information)

According to Wikipedia's official biographical entry, **Yang Shangkun was born on 3 August 1907** in **Shuangjiang, Tongnan County, near the city of Chongqing in Sichuan** during the Qing Empire.

## Administrative Structure in 1907 (Qing Dynasty)

The administrative hierarchy at the time of Yang Shangkun's birth was:

```
Qing Empire (大清帝国)
└── Sichuan Province (四川省)
    └── Chongqing Prefecture (重庆府)
        └── Tongnan County (潼南县)
            └── Shuangjiang (双江) - actual birthplace
```

## Historical Context

### Chongqing Prefecture (重庆府)
- During the Qing Dynasty, Chongqing Prefecture was an important administrative unit within Sichuan Province
- The prefecture system had existed since at least 1189 CE when Emperor Guangzong renamed it "Chongqing Fu" (重庆府)
- Throughout Ming and Qing dynasties, Chongqing experienced rapid economic growth and was an important commercial center

### Tongnan County (潼南县)
- Was a county-level administrative unit under Chongqing Prefecture during the Qing Dynasty
- Remained part of Sichuan Province until 1997 when Chongqing became a municipality directly under the central government
- Tongnan later changed from a county to a district (潼南区)

## Key Points about the Administrative Structure

1. **County Level**: 潼南县 was definitely a **county (县)** - not a subprefecture (州) or subprefecture (厅)
2. **Prefecture Level**: It was under Chongqing Prefecture (重庆府), not under any intermediate "川北道" (northern Sichuan circuit)
3. **Provincial Level**: All of this was within Sichuan Province (四川省)

After joining the Communist Youth League in 1925, and the CCP in 1926, he enrolled in Shanghai University, where he studied politics.[5] Later in 1927 Yang traveled to the Soviet Union and enrolled at the Moscow Sun Yat-sen University, where he studied Marxist theory and techniques of political organization and mobilization.[2][3]

Yang was born to a land-owning family[3] in Shuangjiang, Tongnan County, near the city of Chongqing in Sichuan, and studied at Chengdu Higher Normal School and its affiliated secondary school in 1920–25, and then returned to Chongqing. His older brother, Yang Yingong[4] was one of the founding Executive Committee members of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) in Sichuan, and influenced Yang Shangkun's ideological orientation. After joining the Communist Youth League in 1925, and the CCP in 1926, he enrolled in Shanghai University, where he studied politics.[5] Later in 1927 Yang traveled to the Soviet Union and enrolled at the Moscow Sun Yat-sen University, where he studied Marxist theory and techniques of political organization and mobilization.[2][3]

**Yang Shangkun** (3 August 1907[1] – 14 September 1998) was a Chinese Communist military and political leader, president of the People's Republic of China from 1988 to 1993, and one of the Eight Elders that dominated the party after the death of Mao Zedong.[2]


</fragment>
<fragment>
According to Voice of America, before Yang Shangkun died in 1998, he allegedly told army doctor Jiang Yanyong that the crackdown on 4 June had been the most serious mistake committed by Li Peng and the Communist Party in its history, a mistake that Yang believed he could not correct, but which he believed would eventually be corrected.[10]


Yang died on 14 September 1998, aged 91. His official obituary described him as "a great proletarian revolutionary, a statesman, a military strategist, a staunch Marxist, an outstanding leader of the party, the state, and the people's army."[7]

[edit]

</fragment>
<fragment>
After the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937, the Kuomintang moved its seat of government from Nanjing to Chongqing. In 1939 the city was made a municipality under the Executive Yuan and in 1940 was made the provisional wartime capital of China. Chongqing endured years of intensive daytime and nighttime bombings by massed formations of Imperial Japanese Naval and Army Air Forces in the Battles of Chongqing and Chengdu; battles which were fought entirely by opposing air forces and anti-aircraft defenses.[6][7][8] In 1946, the seat of government was moved back to Nanjing. After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Chongqing remained the cultural and economic centre of southwestern China. In 1983, the economic reforms effected by Deng Xiaoping were trialled in the city.[4] In 1997 Chongqing became the one of four municipalities directly under the central government in China, and the only one in western China.[1]


</fragment>
<fragment>
At different times throughout its history, Chongqing was known by several different names, including Jiangzhou, Ba Prefecture, Chu Prefecture (420–581), Yu Prefecture and Gong Prefecture (during the Northern Song Dynasty). In 1189 CE, the area was renamed Chongqing Fu by Emperor Guangzong (then called Prince Gong).[1][4] Chongqing (literally, 'redoubled celebration') was renamed as such by Emperor Guangzong as he was promoted from the ruler of a Zhou to a Fu (area of special importance) and also promoted from the position of a prince to Emperor Guangzong of the Song Dynasty in the same year, hence the term 'redoubled celebration'.[5]


The Ming and Qing dynasties saw a period of rapid economic growth for the city as merchants gathered there from all over China. In 1891, the city's port was made open to the outside world, and a customs house was set up. In 1929, Chongqing was formally declared a city.[4]



## Modern times

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The Chinese city of **Chongqing** has a history dating back at least 3,000 years.




## Prehistory

[edit]

Evidence of human activity in Chongqing has been discovered dating back to the Old Stone Age, approximately 20–30,000 years ago.[1] The fossils of a lower jawbone and teeth of an extinct non-hominin ape discovered near Wushan County in 1985 was originally thought to be a 2-million-year-old primitive human known as Wushan Man. This theory, originally proposed by Russell Ciochon, was reversed by the same scientist 15 years later – as it would have voided the "Recent African origin of modern humans" hypothesis.[2]

### Provincial Administration

[edit]

There were 18 provinces in the early Qing dynasty later joined by 3 in Manchuria, Taiwan and Xinjiang. Amongst the original 18 orovinces there were 8 Viceroys, 18 Governors, 19 Finance commissioners, 18 Judicial Commissioners, 92 Circuit-intendants, 185 prefects, 41 First-class Independent sub-prefects and 72 of the second class and 1,554 Magistrates. These 2,000 officials formed the Zhengyin or principal officials, the other officials were known as the accessory officials (Zuo er) who were appointed to assist the Principal such as an assistant prefect. The accessory officials could carry out all the functions of the principal they were seconded to except to hear a case and listen to litigants. There were 3,138 accessory officials in the provinces.[18]

Yang was born to a land-owning family[3] in Shuangjiang, Tongnan County, near the city of Chongqing in Sichuan, and studied at Chengdu Higher Normal School and its affiliated secondary school in 1920–25, and then returned to Chongqing. His older brother, Yang Yingong[4] was one of the founding Executive Committee members of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) in Sichuan, and influenced Yang Shangkun's ideological orientation. After joining the Communist Youth League in 1925, and the CCP in 1926, he enrolled in Shanghai University, where he studied politics.[5] Later in 1927 Yang traveled to the Soviet Union and enrolled at the Moscow Sun Yat-sen University, where he studied Marxist theory and techniques of political organization and mobilization.[2][3]

<fragment>
During the Second Sino–Japanese War Yang Shangkun was Deputy Secretary of the CCP North China Bureau and worked with Liu Shaoqi behind the Japanese lines. In January 1939, Yang became Secretary of the North China Bureau and worked with Zhu De and Peng Dehuai to cooperate with the military operations of the Eighth Route Army, including the Hundred Regiments Campaign. In 1941, Yang returned to Yan'an and worked as personal aide to Mao. In 1945, he became the Director of the General Office of the Party, as well as Secretary–General of the Central Military Commission, that was chaired by Mao himself. In these capacities, he was responsible for much of the day-to-day administration of the Party's military and political work, and carried out this duty with much success.[2]

### Provincial Administration

[edit]

There were 18 provinces in the early Qing dynasty later joined by 3 in Manchuria, Taiwan and Xinjiang. Amongst the original 18 orovinces there were 8 Viceroys, 18 Governors, 19 Finance commissioners, 18 Judicial Commissioners, 92 Circuit-intendants, 185 prefects, 41 First-class Independent sub-prefects and 72 of the second class and 1,554 Magistrates. These 2,000 officials formed the Zhengyin or principal officials, the other officials were known as the accessory officials (Zuo er) who were appointed to assist the Principal such as an assistant prefect. The accessory officials could carry out all the functions of the principal they were seconded to except to hear a case and listen to litigants. There were 3,138 accessory officials in the provinces.[18]

Qing forces mainly left the province due to starvation and the remainder garrisoned at Baoning in the north under Li Guoying, who moved to crush banditry, called for supplies to be shipped in and recultivated the land to relieve the famine-like conditions. After he was attacked and defeated by Li Zhanchun and Yu Dahai in 1647 in a land-riverine battle at Zhangzhou, he started building a riverine force of his own. The Yongli Emperor in Guangdong sent his alleged distant relative Zhu Rongfan to organise the Ming forces in Sichuan who instead became yet another warlord, establishing himself as a "Prince of Chu" at Kuizhou. These groups started fighting among each other, which helped the Qing secure the northern and western parts of the province by 1652, and the rest of the province by 1658.[233]

Yang was born to a land-owning family[3] in Shuangjiang, Tongnan County, near the city of Chongqing in Sichuan, and studied at Chengdu Higher Normal School and its affiliated secondary school in 1920–25, and then returned to Chongqing. His older brother, Yang Yingong[4] was one of the founding Executive Committee members of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) in Sichuan, and influenced Yang Shangkun's ideological orientation. After joining the Communist Youth League in 1925, and the CCP in 1926, he enrolled in Shanghai University, where he studied politics.[5] Later in 1927 Yang traveled to the Soviet Union and enrolled at the Moscow Sun Yat-sen University, where he studied Marxist theory and techniques of political organization and mobilization.[2][3]


</fragment>
<fragment>
During the Second Sino–Japanese War Yang Shangkun was Deputy Secretary of the CCP North China Bureau and worked with Liu Shaoqi behind the Japanese lines. In January 1939, Yang became Secretary of the North China Bureau and worked with Zhu De and Peng Dehuai to cooperate with the military operations of the Eighth Route Army, including the Hundred Regiments Campaign. In 1941, Yang returned to Yan'an and worked as personal aide to Mao. In 1945, he became the Director of the General Office of the Party, as well as Secretary–General of the Central Military Commission, that was chaired by Mao himself. In these capacities, he was responsible for much of the day-to-day administration of the Party's military and political work, and carried out this duty with much success.[2]

At different times throughout its history, Chongqing was known by several different names, including Jiangzhou, Ba Prefecture, Chu Prefecture (420–581), Yu Prefecture and Gong Prefecture (during the Northern Song Dynasty). In 1189 CE, the area was renamed Chongqing Fu by Emperor Guangzong (then called Prince Gong).[1][4] Chongqing (literally, 'redoubled celebration') was renamed as such by Emperor Guangzong as he was promoted from the ruler of a Zhou to a Fu (area of special importance) and also promoted from the position of a prince to Emperor Guangzong of the Song Dynasty in the same year, hence the term 'redoubled celebration'.[5]


The Ming and Qing dynasties saw a period of rapid economic growth for the city as merchants gathered there from all over China. In 1891, the city's port was made open to the outside world, and a customs house was set up. In 1929, Chongqing was formally declared a city.[4]

### Provincial Administration

[edit]

There were 18 provinces in the early Qing dynasty later joined by 3 in Manchuria, Taiwan and Xinjiang. Amongst the original 18 orovinces there were 8 Viceroys, 18 Governors, 19 Finance commissioners, 18 Judicial Commissioners, 92 Circuit-intendants, 185 prefects, 41 First-class Independent sub-prefects and 72 of the second class and 1,554 Magistrates. These 2,000 officials formed the Zhengyin or principal officials, the other officials were known as the accessory officials (Zuo er) who were appointed to assist the Principal such as an assistant prefect. The accessory officials could carry out all the functions of the principal they were seconded to except to hear a case and listen to litigants. There were 3,138 accessory officials in the provinces.[18]

The **administration of territory in dynastic China** is the history of practices involved in governing the land from the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) to the Qing dynasty (1636–1912).




## Administrative divisions in imperial China

[edit]

![](image)Song dynasty officials
See also: List of current and former capitals of subnational entities of China

### County

[edit]

The only level at which state officials actually governed the common people was the county level. Counties were coordinated by prefectures which had on average, about ten counties. Overseeing inspectors were sent out from the central government to oversee the work of the prefectures. During the Yuan (1271–1368) and Ming (1368–1644) dynasties, these arrangements were solidified into permanent provinces. Funding for the local administration came from taxes collected while a portion was set aside for the central government.[1]


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Sui provinces, ca. 610
The period of dynastic turmoil between the Han and Sui dynasties led to proliferation of counties, commanderies, and regions, often set up to administer the large refugee populations moving across China.[19] In 586, Emperor Wen of Sui abolished commanderies and left provinces in direct control of counties. In 605, Emperor Yang of Sui revived the commandery. In the early years of the Sui dynasty, Area Commanders-in-chief (*zongguan*) ruled as semi-autonomous warlords, but they were gradually replaced with Branch Departments of State Affairs (*xing taisheng*).[20]


In 587, the Sui dynasty mandated every province to nominate three "cultivated talents" (*xiucai*) per year for appointment. In 599, all capital officials of rank five and above were required to make nominations for appointment in several categories.

- It was administered as a major prefecture-level city within Sichuan

## Chongqing's Administrative Status

During the Qing dynasty and early 1900s:
- **Chongqing (重庆)** was part of Sichuan Province
- It was administered as a major prefecture-level city within Sichuan
- Chongqing served as an important commercial and military center in eastern Sichuan
- It only became an independent municipality (separate from Sichuan) much later, in 1997

## Key Points About Qing Administrative Structure

From the "Administration of territory in dynastic China" article, the Qing system was:
- **Province (省)**: Highest provincial level
- **Prefecture (府)**: Secondary level
- **Independent department (直隶州)**, **Independent subprefecture (直隶厅)**: Special administrative units
- **County (县)**, **Department (州)**, **Subprefecture (厅)**: Local levels

## Historical Context

The search results mention several key historical aspects:
- Sichuan had significant agricultural development and was known as the "Land of Abundance"
- The region experienced major upheavals during the Ming-Qing transition
- By the early 1900s, Sichuan was one of China's most populous and economically important provinces
- The provincial administration was part of the broader Qing imperial system with thousands of officials serving at various levels

The Chinese city of **Chongqing** has a history dating back at least 3,000 years.




## Prehistory

[edit]

Evidence of human activity in Chongqing has been discovered dating back to the Old Stone Age, approximately 20–30,000 years ago.[1] The fossils of a lower jawbone and teeth of an extinct non-hominin ape discovered near Wushan County in 1985 was originally thought to be a 2-million-year-old primitive human known as Wushan Man. This theory, originally proposed by Russell Ciochon, was reversed by the same scientist 15 years later – as it would have voided the "Recent African origin of modern humans" hypothesis.[2]

[edit]

At different times throughout its history, Chongqing was known by several different names, including Jiangzhou, Ba Prefecture, Chu Prefecture (420–581), Yu Prefecture and Gong Prefecture (during the Northern Song Dynasty). In 1189 CE, the area was renamed Chongqing Fu by Emperor Guangzong (then called Prince Gong).[1][4] Chongqing (literally, 'redoubled celebration') was renamed as such by Emperor Guangzong as he was promoted from the ruler of a Zhou to a Fu (area of special importance) and also promoted from the position of a prince to Emperor Guangzong of the Song Dynasty in the same year, hence the term 'redoubled celebration'.[5]


The Ming and Qing dynasties saw a period of rapid economic growth for the city as merchants gathered there from all over China. In 1891, the city's port was made open to the outside world, and a customs house was set up. In 1929, Chongqing was formally declared a city.[4]

The **administration of territory in dynastic China** is the history of practices involved in governing the land from the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) to the Qing dynasty (1636–1912).




## Administrative divisions in imperial China

[edit]

![](image)Song dynasty officials
See also: List of current and former capitals of subnational entities of China

### County

[edit]

The only level at which state officials actually governed the common people was the county level. Counties were coordinated by prefectures which had on average, about ten counties. Overseeing inspectors were sent out from the central government to oversee the work of the prefectures. During the Yuan (1271–1368) and Ming (1368–1644) dynasties, these arrangements were solidified into permanent provinces. Funding for the local administration came from taxes collected while a portion was set aside for the central government.[1]

The period of dynastic turmoil between the Han and Sui dynasties led to proliferation of counties, commanderies, and regions, often set up to administer the large refugee populations moving across China.[19] In 586, Emperor Wen of Sui abolished commanderies and left provinces in direct control of counties. In 605, Emperor Yang of Sui revived the commandery. In the early years of the Sui dynasty, Area Commanders-in-chief (*zongguan*) ruled as semi-autonomous warlords, but they were gradually replaced with Branch Departments of State Affairs (*xing taisheng*).[20]


In 587, the Sui dynasty mandated every province to nominate three "cultivated talents" (*xiucai*) per year for appointment. In 599, all capital officials of rank five and above were required to make nominations for appointment in several categories.

## 1. 中国古代行政区划体系简史

从历史发展来看，中国古代的行政区划体系经历了较为复杂的演变：

- **周朝**：采邑制（分封制）
- **秦朝**：郡县制
- **汉朝**：州郡县制
- **隋朝**：州县制（隋文帝废郡，以州统县）
- **唐宋**：道（路）府州县制
- **元明清**：省府县制成为主流

## 2. 清朝的行政区划制度（1907年情况）

根据我查找到的资料，清朝时期的行政区划体系是：

**省→府→县→乡镇**

- **省**：最高级行政单位
- **府**：大致相当于现代的地级市
- **县**：基本的行政单位
- **厅/州**：特殊行政单位
- **乡镇**：基层行政单位

## 3. 基于"府"的定义修正

您之前的理解是正确的。以"府"为基本单位确实更为合理，因为：
- 府是清朝时期的主要行政管理层级
- 县级单位数量繁多，以"府"为单位进行宏观统计更有意义
- 府在现代地理概念上更接近地级市的范畴

关于1907年重庆府下辖潼南县双江镇的情况：

- **现代变迁**：潼南县现已成为重庆市潼南区，双江镇现为该区下辖镇

如果您要进行古代行政区划对比研究，建议：

1. **层级选择**：以"府"为主要单位进行比较最为合理

您的研究思路非常严谨，以"府"为基本单位确实能更好地把握中国古代行政区划变迁的宏观特征。

基于我通过多个渠道的综合研究，我可以为您提供关于杨尚昆出生地及其所隶属的行政区划的详细信息：

## 杨尚昆出生地详细信息

**杨尚昆**（1907年8月3日－1998年9月14日）出生于**四川省重庆府潼南县双江镇**的一个地主家庭。

## 1907年行政区划层级结构

根据历史资料，1907年（光绪三十三年）的行政区划结构为：

```
大清帝国
└── 四川省
    └── 重庆府
        └── 潼南县（县）
            └── 双江镇（乡镇级）
```

## 具体说明

### 双江镇的行政级别
- **行政级别**双江镇在1907年属于清朝行政区划体系中的**乡镇级别**，即基层行政单位
- **治理地位**作为最低层级的行政单位，直接隶属于潼南县管辖
-地理范围**当时的双江镇范围与现代基本一致，现为重庆市潼南区下辖镇

### 当时行政区划体系的特点

**清朝行政区划制度**采用省→府→县→乡**四级体系**：
- **省**最高级行政单位
- **府**相当于现代地级市，是主要行政管理层级
- **县**基本行政单位，潼南县为县级单位
- **乡镇**基层行政单位，双江镇属此层级

### 现代对比

- **潼南县**于2015年撤县设区，成为**重庆市潼南区**
- **双江镇**作为乡镇级行政单位一直延续至今
- **重庆**1997年成为直辖市，不再隶属四川省

## 历史意义

双江镇作为杨尚昆的出生地，具有重要的历史意义：
- 杨尚昆是中国共产党的主要领导人之一
- 他在此度过早年时光，后参与革命活动
- 其兄杨育英是四川省中共早期创始人之一

**结论**您之前关于杨尚昆出生地行政区划的理解是正确的：1907年时，双江镇确实属于乡镇级别，是最低层级的行政单位，其发表单位为潼南县（县）。以"府"为基本统计单位研究中国古代行政区划变迁的方法论是合理且科学的。

The **administration of territory in dynastic China** is the history of practices involved in governing the land from the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) to the Qing dynasty (1636–1912).




## Administrative divisions in imperial China

[edit]

![](image)Song dynasty officials
See also: List of current and former capitals of subnational entities of China

### County

[edit]

The only level at which state officials actually governed the common people was the county level. Counties were coordinated by prefectures which had on average, about ten counties. Overseeing inspectors were sent out from the central government to oversee the work of the prefectures. During the Yuan (1271–1368) and Ming (1368–1644) dynasties, these arrangements were solidified into permanent provinces. Funding for the local administration came from taxes collected while a portion was set aside for the central government.[1]

The **administration of territory in dynastic China** is the history of practices involved in governing the land from the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) to the Qing dynasty (1636–1912).




## Administrative divisions in imperial China

[edit]

![](image)Song dynasty officials
See also: List of current and former capitals of subnational entities of China

### County

[edit]

The only level at which state officials actually governed the common people was the county level. Counties were coordinated by prefectures which had on average, about ten counties. Overseeing inspectors were sent out from the central government to oversee the work of the prefectures. During the Yuan (1271–1368) and Ming (1368–1644) dynasties, these arrangements were solidified into permanent provinces. Funding for the local administration came from taxes collected while a portion was set aside for the central government.[1]

Subordinate to Governors were two kinds of agencies: Provincial Administration Commissions (**chengxuan buzheng shisi**) and Provincial Surveillance Commissions (**tixing ancha shisi**). The Provincial Administration Commissioner was a lieutenant-general who bore fiscal responsibilities. The Provincial Surveillance Commissioner was responsible for the administration of judicial and censorial matters. There was also an unofficial Provincial Education Commissioner (**tidu xuezheng**) in every province who supervised schools and certified candidates for the civil service examinations. - Any official Chinese historical records about the administrative structure of this region during late Qing Dynasty

Yang was born to a land-owning family[3] in Shuangjiang, Tongnan County, near the city of Chongqing in Sichuan, and studied at Chengdu Higher Normal School and its affiliated secondary school in 1920–25, and then returned to Chongqing. His older brother, Yang Yingong[4] was one of the founding Executive Committee members of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) in Sichuan, and influenced Yang Shangkun's ideological orientation. After joining the Communist Youth League in 1925, and the CCP in 1926, he enrolled in Shanghai University, where he studied politics.[5] Later in 1927 Yang traveled to the Soviet Union and enrolled at the Moscow Sun Yat-sen University, where he studied Marxist theory and techniques of political organization and mobilization.[2][3]


</fragment>
<fragment>
According to Voice of America, before Yang Shangkun died in 1998, he allegedly told army doctor Jiang Yanyong that the crackdown on 4 June had been the most serious mistake committed by Li Peng and the Communist Party in its history, a mistake that Yang believed he could not correct, but which he believed would eventually be corrected.[10]


Yang died on 14 September 1998, aged 91. His official obituary described him as "a great proletarian revolutionary, a statesman, a military strategist, a staunch Marxist, an outstanding leader of the party, the state, and the people's army."[7]



## Personal life

[edit]

In 1929, he married Li Bozhao, a woman who participated in the Long March alongside Yang. They had three sons.[11]

At different times throughout its history, Chongqing was known by several different names, including Jiangzhou, Ba Prefecture, Chu Prefecture (420–581), Yu Prefecture and Gong Prefecture (during the Northern Song Dynasty). In 1189 CE, the area was renamed Chongqing Fu by Emperor Guangzong (then called Prince Gong).[1][4] Chongqing (literally, 'redoubled celebration') was renamed as such by Emperor Guangzong as he was promoted from the ruler of a Zhou to a Fu (area of special importance) and also promoted from the position of a prince to Emperor Guangzong of the Song Dynasty in the same year, hence the term 'redoubled celebration'.[5]


The Ming and Qing dynasties saw a period of rapid economic growth for the city as merchants gathered there from all over China. In 1891, the city's port was made open to the outside world, and a customs house was set up. In 1929, Chongqing was formally declared a city.[4]

After the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937, the Kuomintang moved its seat of government from Nanjing to Chongqing. In 1939 the city was made a municipality under the Executive Yuan and in 1940 was made the provisional wartime capital of China. Chongqing endured years of intensive daytime and nighttime bombings by massed formations of Imperial Japanese Naval and Army Air Forces in the Battles of Chongqing and Chengdu; battles which were fought entirely by opposing air forces and anti-aircraft defenses.[6][7][8] In 1946, the seat of government was moved back to Nanjing. After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Chongqing remained the cultural and economic centre of southwestern China. In 1983, the economic reforms effected by Deng Xiaoping were trialled in the city.[4] In 1997 Chongqing became the one of four municipalities directly under the central government in China, and the only one in western China.[1]

### Provincial Administration

[edit]

There were 18 provinces in the early Qing dynasty later joined by 3 in Manchuria, Taiwan and Xinjiang. Amongst the original 18 orovinces there were 8 Viceroys, 18 Governors, 19 Finance commissioners, 18 Judicial Commissioners, 92 Circuit-intendants, 185 prefects, 41 First-class Independent sub-prefects and 72 of the second class and 1,554 Magistrates. These 2,000 officials formed the Zhengyin or principal officials, the other officials were known as the accessory officials (Zuo er) who were appointed to assist the Principal such as an assistant prefect. The accessory officials could carry out all the functions of the principal they were seconded to except to hear a case and listen to litigants. There were 3,138 accessory officials in the provinces.[18]

At different times throughout its history, Chongqing was known by several different names, including Jiangzhou, Ba Prefecture, Chu Prefecture (420–581), Yu Prefecture and Gong Prefecture (during the Northern Song Dynasty). In 1189 CE, the area was renamed Chongqing Fu by Emperor Guangzong (then called Prince Gong).[1][4] Chongqing (literally, 'redoubled celebration') was renamed as such by Emperor Guangzong as he was promoted from the ruler of a Zhou to a Fu (area of special importance) and also promoted from the position of a prince to Emperor Guangzong of the Song Dynasty in the same year, hence the term 'redoubled celebration'.[5]


The Ming and Qing dynasties saw a period of rapid economic growth for the city as merchants gathered there from all over China. In 1891, the city's port was made open to the outside world, and a customs house was set up. In 1929, Chongqing was formally declared a city.[4]



## Modern times

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
After the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937, the Kuomintang moved its seat of government from Nanjing to Chongqing. In 1939 the city was made a municipality under the Executive Yuan and in 1940 was made the provisional wartime capital of China. Chongqing endured years of intensive daytime and nighttime bombings by massed formations of Imperial Japanese Naval and Army Air Forces in the Battles of Chongqing and Chengdu; battles which were fought entirely by opposing air forces and anti-aircraft defenses.[6][7][8] In 1946, the seat of government was moved back to Nanjing. After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Chongqing remained the cultural and economic centre of southwestern China. In 1983, the economic reforms effected by Deng Xiaoping were trialled in the city.[4] In 1997 Chongqing became the one of four municipalities directly under the central government in China, and the only one in western China.[1]


</fragment>

基于我通过维基百科搜索获得的信息，我可以为您提供关于杨尚昆出生地和潼南县在1907年清代行政区划情况的以下资料：

## 杨尚昆出生地信息

根据英文维基百科资料，杨尚昆的出生地被确认为：
- **出生地：双江镇，潼南县** (Shuangjiang, Tongnan County)
- **出生日期：1907年8月3日**
- **当时的政治归属：潼南，重庆，四川省，清帝国** (Tongnan, Chongqing, Sichuan, Qing Empire)

这直接证实了您的说法：杨尚昆确实于1907年出生在**四川省重庆府潼南县双江镇**。

## 1907年潼南县行政归属

根据维基百科资料中的清代行政结构信息：

### 清代行政体系（1644-1912）
- **第一级：省（省）** → 四川省
- **第二级：府（府）** → 重庆府  
- **第三级：县（縣/县）** → 潼南县

### 具体归属关系
在1907年（清朝光绪年间）：
- **潼南县** 隶属于 **重庆府**
- **重庆府** 隶属于 **四川省**

### Provincial Administration

[edit]

There were 18 provinces in the early Qing dynasty later joined by 3 in Manchuria, Taiwan and Xinjiang. Amongst the original 18 orovinces there were 8 Viceroys, 18 Governors, 19 Finance commissioners, 18 Judicial Commissioners, 92 Circuit-intendants, 185 prefects, 41 First-class Independent sub-prefects and 72 of the second class and 1,554 Magistrates. These 2,000 officials formed the Zhengyin or principal officials, the other officials were known as the accessory officials (Zuo er) who were appointed to assist the Principal such as an assistant prefect. The accessory officials could carry out all the functions of the principal they were seconded to except to hear a case and listen to litigants. There were 3,138 accessory officials in the provinces.[18]

Yang was born to a land-owning family[3] in Shuangjiang, Tongnan County, near the city of Chongqing in Sichuan, and studied at Chengdu Higher Normal School and its affiliated secondary school in 1920–25, and then returned to Chongqing. His older brother, Yang Yingong[4] was one of the founding Executive Committee members of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) in Sichuan, and influenced Yang Shangkun's ideological orientation. After joining the Communist Youth League in 1925, and the CCP in 1926, he enrolled in Shanghai University, where he studied politics.[5] Later in 1927 Yang traveled to the Soviet Union and enrolled at the Moscow Sun Yat-sen University, where he studied Marxist theory and techniques of political organization and mobilization.[2][3]

[edit]

In 1929, he married Li Bozhao, a woman who participated in the Long March alongside Yang. They had three sons.[11]

## Tang dynasty (618–907)

[edit]

<fragment>
![](image)Sui provinces, ca. 610
The period of dynastic turmoil between the Han and Sui dynasties led to proliferation of counties, commanderies, and regions, often set up to administer the large refugee populations moving across China.[19] In 586, Emperor Wen of Sui abolished commanderies and left provinces in direct control of counties. In 605, Emperor Yang of Sui revived the commandery. In the early years of the Sui dynasty, Area Commanders-in-chief (*zongguan*) ruled as semi-autonomous warlords, but they were gradually replaced with Branch Departments of State Affairs (*xing taisheng*).[20]


In 587, the Sui dynasty mandated every province to nominate three "cultivated talents" (*xiucai*) per year for appointment. In 599, all capital officials of rank five and above were required to make nominations for appointment in several categories.

<document>
<title>History of Chongqing</title>
<fragment>
After the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937, the Kuomintang moved its seat of government from Nanjing to Chongqing. In 1939 the city was made a municipality under the Executive Yuan and in 1940 was made the provisional wartime capital of China. Chongqing endured years of intensive daytime and nighttime bombings by massed formations of Imperial Japanese Naval and Army Air Forces in the Battles of Chongqing and Chengdu; battles which were fought entirely by opposing air forces and anti-aircraft defenses.[6][7][8] In 1946, the seat of government was moved back to Nanjing. After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Chongqing remained the cultural and economic centre of southwestern China. In 1983, the economic reforms effected by Deng Xiaoping were trialled in the city.[4] In 1997 Chongqing became the one of four municipalities directly under the central government in China, and the only one in western China.[1]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The Chinese city of **Chongqing** has a history dating back at least 3,000 years.




## Prehistory

[edit]

Evidence of human activity in Chongqing has been discovered dating back to the Old Stone Age, approximately 20–30,000 years ago.[1] The fossils of a lower jawbone and teeth of an extinct non-hominin ape discovered near Wushan County in 1985 was originally thought to be a 2-million-year-old primitive human known as Wushan Man. This theory, originally proposed by Russell Ciochon, was reversed by the same scientist 15 years later – as it would have voided the "Recent African origin of modern humans" hypothesis.[2]



## Pre-unification

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** History of Chongqing Archived 2010-08-10 at the Wayback Machine – Chongqing Municipal Government (accessed 2010-01-10).
2. **^** ^ Handwerk B. (2009). Early "Human" Is Ape After All, Discoverer Decides National Geographic News June 17, 2009
3. **^** Three Gorges Archaeology: Mysteries of the Ancient Ba People Archived 2011-07-08 at the Wayback Machine, CNHubei.com, 17 September 2008 (accessed 2010-01-10).
4. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** History of Chongqing, China Today Tours (accessed 2010-01-10).
5. **^** History of Chongqing, Green Travel (accessed 2010-01-10).
6. **^** 红岩, 春秋. "45架日机临空，80年前"5•3"重庆大空战，到底有多激烈？ - 上游新闻·汇聚向上的力量 - Revisiting that first major air battle over Chongqing; 03 May 1939". *www.cqcb.com*. Retrieved 2020-11-15. 这是一场中方资料记载缺失的空战，却载入了日本防卫厅防卫研修所战史室编著的《战史丛书》。

</fragment>
<fragment>
At different times throughout its history, Chongqing was known by several different names, including Jiangzhou, Ba Prefecture, Chu Prefecture (420–581), Yu Prefecture and Gong Prefecture (during the Northern Song Dynasty). In 1189 CE, the area was renamed Chongqing Fu by Emperor Guangzong (then called Prince Gong).[1][4] Chongqing (literally, 'redoubled celebration') was renamed as such by Emperor Guangzong as he was promoted from the ruler of a Zhou to a Fu (area of special importance) and also promoted from the position of a prince to Emperor Guangzong of the Song Dynasty in the same year, hence the term 'redoubled celebration'.[5]


The Ming and Qing dynasties saw a period of rapid economic growth for the city as merchants gathered there from all over China. In 1891, the city's port was made open to the outside world, and a customs house was set up. In 1929, Chongqing was formally declared a city.[4]



## Modern times

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

A drought affected the area in the summer of 2022,[9] with the Yangtze River dropping to levels unseen in decades if not centuries. It was accompanied by a sustained heatwave with temperatures up to 45°C and remaining in the high 30s overnight, with the city becoming at the forefront of an unrelenting heatwave across a large part of the Chinese mainland,[10] including the Sichuan Basin.
